case_info.scenario: A 64-year-old man with a 2-year history of seizure disorder presented to the emergency department (ED) at an outside hospital with breakthrough seizures. One month prior to his ED visit, he had been treated with oral antibiotics when he presented to an urgent care center with left-sided otorrhea, otalgia, and hearing loss. In the ED, he denied headaches, fever, otalgia, otorrhea, or hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast showed diffuse enhancement and possible coalescence in the left mastoid process with adjacent dural enhancement and sigmoid sinus occlusion. He received intravenous vancomycin and cefepime and was started on a heparin drip before being transferred to our facility. On presentation at our facility, the patient appeared well with normal vital signs. There was no periauricular swelling or erythema. Otoscopic examination showed no inflammation of the external auditory canals, and the tympanic membranes were translucent without evidence of retraction or effusion. Computed tomographic venogram confirmed occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and computed tomography of the temporal bone showed coalescence of mastoid air cells with erosion into the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was performed for biopsy and culture specimens. Histologic findings from the specimens demonstrated cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm arranged in syncytial clusters with occasional whorls, pseudoinclusions, and psammomatous calcifications (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical stains were positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and vimentin (Figure, B).

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

}

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast showed diffuse enhancement and possible coalescence in the left mastoid process with adjacent dural enhancement and sigmoid sinus occlusion. He received intravenous vancomycin and cefepime and was started on a heparin drip before being transferred to our facility. On presentation at our facility, the patient appeared well with normal vital signs. There was no periauricular swelling or erythema. Otoscopic examination showed no inflammation of the external auditory canals, and the tympanic membranes were translucent without evidence of retraction or effusion. Computed tomographic venogram confirmed occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and computed tomography of the temporal bone showed coalescence of mastoid air cells with erosion into the sigmoid sinus. Histologic findings from the specimens demonstrated cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm arranged in syncytial clusters with occasional whorls, pseudoinclusions, and psammomatous calcifications (Figure, A). case_info.scenario: A 64-year-old man with a 2-year history of seizure disorder presented to the emergency department (ED) at an outside hospital with breakthrough seizures. One month prior to his ED visit, he had been treated with oral antibiotics when he presented to an urgent care center with left-sided otorrhea, otalgia, and hearing loss. In the ED, he denied headaches, fever, otalgia, otorrhea, or hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast showed diffuse enhancement and possible coalescence in the left mastoid process with adjacent dural enhancement and sigmoid sinus occlusion. He received intravenous vancomycin and cefepime and was started on a heparin drip before being transferred to our facility. On presentation at our facility, the patient appeared well with normal vital signs. There was no periauricular swelling or erythema. Otoscopic examination showed no inflammation of the external auditory canals, and the tympanic membranes were translucent without evidence of retraction or effusion. Computed tomographic venogram confirmed occlusion of the left transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and computed tomography of the temporal bone showed coalescence of mastoid air cells with erosion into the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was performed for biopsy and culture specimens. Histologic findings from the specimens demonstrated cells with oval nuclei and abundant cytoplasm arranged in syncytial clusters with occasional whorls, pseudoinclusions, and psammomatous calcifications (Figure, A). Immunohistochemical stains were positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) and vimentin (Figure, B).

options.C: Acute coalescent mastoiditis with sigmoid sinus thrombosis

distractors: Acute coalescent mastoiditis with sigmoid sinus thrombosis
case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

case_info.caption: Hematoxylin-eosin stain (A) and immunohistochemical stain (B) after mastoidectomy for biopsy and culture specimens.
case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10

case_info.explanation: This patient presented to the ED with an acute exacerbation of a seizure disorder. The recent history of left-sided otorrhea and otalgia with magnetic resonance imaging enhancement in the mastoid along with dehiscence and occlusion of the adjacent venous sinuses suggested that the seizure may have been triggered by an indolent suppurative complication of mastoiditis. However, because the patient’s otologic symptoms had resolved and he did not appear septic, temporal bone neoplasm was considered. Mastoidectomy revealed solid tumor attached to the sigmoid sinus with no evidence of mastoid suppuration or inflammatory process, and the biopsy was diagnostic for intraosseous meningioma. Meningiomas typically are intracranial neoplasms, but 2% present as extracranial intraosseous lesions.1,2Extracranial meningiomas present in the middle ear, external auditory canal, petrous bone, squamous temporal bone, and paranasal sinuses.1Histologic sections in this case showed findings consistent with a meningothelial variant of meningioma World Health Organization grade I.1,3Immunohistochemistry studies confirmed the diagnosis with positive EMA and vimentin staining.3However, somatostatin receptor subtype 2A and progesterone receptors are more sensitive for diagnosis. Intraosseous meningiomas originate from arachnoid cap cells associated with the sigmoid sinus or adjacent dura. As was the case with this patient, most patients with temporal bone intraosseous meningiomas are asymptomatic, and observation with serial imaging is appropriate. Surgical debulking or resection is considered when tumors grow and extend into the middle ear causing hearing loss, compromising patency of the external auditory canal, or compressing the facial nerve. Fractionated external-beam radiation therapy or stereotactic radiation therapy are also options for treating growing tumors, but there is a high risk of profound hearing loss.2 Coalescent mastoiditis can present with intracranial complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis or subperiosteal abscess.4Typically, patients with acute mastoiditis present with headaches, vomiting, seizures, otalgia, otorrhea, and fever.5Physical findings include tenderness and swelling inferior to the temporal line, purulent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Cholesteatoma can be the source of infection in patients with acute mastoiditis, but otomicroscopic findings would reveal a retraction of the tympanic membrane, scutal erosion, or secondary acquired cholesteatoma associated with a tympanic membrane perforation. The absence of these symptoms and physical findings make these diagnoses less likely, yet it is possible to have an indolent progressive suppurative mastoid infection that remains isolated from the middle ear and erodes the thin bony plate over the sigmoid sinus. Mastoidectomy was critical to differentiate an infectious process from neoplastic pathology. Histologic results for a cholesteatoma would reveal keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with stromal fibrosis. Biopsy in patients with mastoiditis shows granulation tissue, acute and chronic leukocyte infiltration, and hemorrhage with negative EMA and vimentin staining. Mastoidectomy in patients with acute coalescent mastoiditis provides drainage of the infection and cultures to select intravenous antibiotics. Anticoagulation may be recommended when acute coalescent mastoiditis results in sigmoid sinus thrombosis.6,7 Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the temporal bone is extremely rare in older adults. Patients present with otorrhea, subjective hearing loss, otalgia, and soft-tissue postauricular swelling.8Physical examination shows granulation tissue in the external ear canal, middle ear effusion, conductive hearing loss, and external auditory canal stenosis.8The absence of these symptoms and physical examination findings make this diagnosis less likely. Computed tomography of the temporal bone shows erosion of mastoid air cells and destruction of the mastoid cortex while the otic capsule is spared.9Computed tomographic imaging is critical for diagnosing and following Langerhans cell histiocytosis, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis. Histological sections typically demonstrate mononuclear cells with coffee bean nuclei that are CD1a, S100, and langerin positive.8,9For focal lesions, surgery is recommended, and for multifocal lesions chemotherapy (typically vincristine and steroids) and surgery is recommended.8,10
